title: Severity, intelligence and adaptive functioning
blurb: Use severity levels and adaptive functioning to plan the right support, and know what PMLD means for nursing care.
question: Gareth, 34, has profound and multiple learning disabilities and is on a respiratory ward with a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 3. His mother says he is 'not himself': quieter, not smiling at her and not turning to music. Staff see no distress. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: A learning disability can be mild, moderate, severe or profound, and in all cases it is lifelong. Mencap describes a person with a mild learning disability as often mixing well with others and coping with most everyday tasks, though they may need help with things like forms. People with a severe learning disability or PMLD need more care and support with mobility, personal care and communication; people with a moderate learning disability may need support in these areas too. In plain English: the level tells you roughly how much help someone needs, never what they are worth.

bands.label: Copes with most daily tasks; help with forms, money, new situations

teach.h: Why an IQ score is not enough
teach.body: An IQ score is a snapshot from one test on one day. Anxiety, illness, sensory loss, communication differences and unfamiliar settings can all lower it. It also tells you little about what a person can do. Adaptive functioning (everyday conceptual, social and practical skills such as self-care, money, travel, safety and communication) is what shapes a support plan. ICD-11 describes both intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour, assessed together.

teach.h: Mild vs profound: different nursing priorities

teach.body: Profound and multiple learning disabilities means a profound learning disability together with physical and/or sensory impairments and complex health needs. Most people with PMLD have very limited or no verbal communication and rely on others for eating, washing and personal care. They communicate through sounds, facial expression, body tone, movement and behaviour, so the people who know them well are essential partners in recognising illness.

teach.h: Scenario: Gareth on the respiratory ward
teach.body: Gareth cannot tell staff he feels worse, and his NEWS2 of 3 does not capture his usual self. His mother knows his baseline: he normally smiles at her and turns to music. A loss of that response is a change from baseline and a soft sign of deterioration. The nurse records her observations, repeats a full set of vital signs, assesses for pain and escalates to the medical team now rather than waiting for the score to rise.

teach.text: Severity is not capacity and not a 'mental age'. A severe learning disability does not mean a person lacks capacity for every decision, and describing an adult as 'having a mental age of five' is inaccurate and devaluing. Describe what the person can do and the support they need.

items: Four levels: mild, moderate, severe, profound; all lifelong.
IQ bands are approximate; adaptive functioning shapes the support plan.
Mild: needs can hide behind fluent speech; check understanding.
PMLD: profound LD + physical/sensory impairment + complex health needs; communication through behaviour.
LeDeR 2023: severe or profound LD, average age at death 58.

summary: You can now describe the four levels of learning disability, explain why adaptive functioning matters more than an IQ score for planning care, and recognise the particular risks for people with mild learning disability and with PMLD. You can use carers' knowledge of a person's baseline to spot deterioration.

A.q: A student nurse asks how Mencap describes a person with a mild learning disability. Which description fits best?
options: Needs support with mobility, personal care and communication
Has very limited speech and complex physical health needs
Copes with most everyday tasks but may need help with forms
Has no support needs and is not covered by adjustments
A.why: Mencap: a person with a mild learning disability will often mix well with others and cope with most everyday tasks, but may need support with things like filling in forms.

whyNot.0: Mencap uses this for people with a severe learning disability or PMLD, and for some people with a moderate learning disability.
whyNot.3: People with a mild learning disability often have needs that are easily missed, and are entitled to reasonable adjustments.

A.q: A healthcare assistant is supporting Amira, 24, who has profound and multiple learning disabilities. How does Amira most likely communicate how she feels?
options: Short spoken sentences using simple words
Sounds, facial expression, body tone and behaviour
Pointing to words on an easy read chart
Writing answers on a whiteboard with prompts
A.why: Most people with PMLD have very limited or no verbal communication and communicate through sounds, facial expression, body tone, movement and behaviour.

whyNot.0: Very limited or no speech is typical in PMLD.
whyNot.2: Reading words is unlikely with a profound learning disability.
whyNot.3: Writing requires literacy and fine motor skills that PMLD usually affects.

A.q: A care home manager wants to use each resident's IQ score to decide how many staff hours they need. Why is this approach flawed?
options: IQ scores rise steadily through adult life
IQ testing measures memory rather than reasoning
IQ scores are confidential to the psychologist
An IQ score says little about the help needed day to day
A.why: Support needs depend on adaptive functioning: what the person can do in self-care, communication, money, travel and safety. An IQ score does not describe these.

whyNot.0: Adult IQ scores do not rise steadily; the issue is that they do not describe daily support needs.
whyNot.1: IQ tests assess a range of reasoning skills; the flaw is their limited link to daily support.
whyNot.2: Scores can be shared with consent where relevant; confidentiality is not the main problem.

B.q: Under ICD-11, how is the severity of a disorder of intellectual development described?
options: By intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour together
By IQ score, with adaptive behaviour used as a tie-breaker
By the underlying cause, such as a named genetic syndrome
By the age at which the diagnosis was first recorded
B.why: ICD-11 grades mild, moderate, severe and profound by how far both intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour fall below the population mean.

whyNot.1: Adaptive behaviour is central, not a tie-breaker.
whyNot.2: The same syndrome can occur with different levels; cause does not set severity.
whyNot.3: The age at diagnosis does not determine severity.

B.q: Callum, 29, has a mild learning disability and lives alone. He has missed three outpatient appointments, and his support worker finds the hospital letters unopened in a drawer. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
options: Discharge him back to his GP under the missed appointments policy
Ask how he manages letters and offer reminders in a format he can use
Refer him for a capacity assessment about attending his appointments
Ask the GP to consider moving him into a residential care home
B.why: Callum's needs are hidden behind his independence: he may not be able to read or act on standard letters. Finding out what works and adjusting (texts, calls, easy read) removes the barrier.

whyNot.0: Discharging him without adjusting the process would disadvantage him because of his disability.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests he lacks capacity; the barrier is how information reaches him.
whyNot.3: He lives independently; a missed letter problem calls for a simple adjustment, not a move.

B.q: LeDeR found that people with a severe or profound learning disability died younger than other people with a learning disability. Which explanation is most relevant to nursing practice?
options: Severity itself shortens life, so these deaths are not avoidable
They decline treatment more often than other patients do
They may not be able to report symptoms, so illness is missed
Annual health checks begin later for people with greater needs
B.why: People with severe and profound learning disability were more likely to die of something treatable. Limited verbal communication means illness can be missed unless staff use baselines and listen to carers.

whyNot.0: LeDeR found many deaths were from treatable causes, so they were not inevitable.
whyNot.1: Refusal is not the explanation LeDeR highlights; missed or delayed recognition is.
whyNot.3: Annual health checks are available to everyone on the GP register from age 14, whatever the severity.

C.q: Gareth, 34, has PMLD and a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 3. His mother says he is quieter than usual, is not smiling at her and does not turn to his music. Staff have seen no distress. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat NEWS2 in four hours, as his score is in the low range
Record that he is settled, as he is showing no signs of distress
Ask for his behaviour support plan to be reviewed by the team
Treat this as a change from baseline and escalate to the doctor
C.why: Gareth cannot report how he feels. His mother knows his baseline, and losing his usual responses is a soft sign of deterioration. Recording, reassessing and escalating now avoids diagnostic overshadowing.

whyNot.0: A low score can understate deterioration in someone whose baseline differs; carer concern needs acting on now.
whyNot.1: Absence of obvious distress does not mean he is well; his responses have changed.
whyNot.2: This is a possible physical deterioration, not a behaviour problem.

C.q: Ruth, 50, has a severe learning disability and needs a tooth extraction. A dental nurse says, 'People with a severe learning disability can't consent, so we'll do a best interests form.' What is the best response?
options: Capacity is decision-specific, so assess this decision with support
Severe learning disability means a best interests decision is needed
Her sister can sign as next of kin, so a form is not required
Capacity depends on her IQ band being above the severe range
C.why: MCA s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a condition. Ruth's capacity is assessed for this decision, after all practicable steps to help her decide.

whyNot.1: Severity alone cannot establish incapacity; a best interests decision follows only an assessment showing she lacks capacity.
whyNot.2: A relative cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
whyNot.3: Capacity is not based on IQ bands but on the functional test for this decision.

C.q: Sian, 40, has PMLD and is fed by gastrostomy. A new team will support her in her home. Which care plan entry most reduces the risk that deterioration is missed?
options: Her weekly activity timetable and favourite music playlists
Her IQ band and diagnosis codes from the original referral
Her usual sounds, colour, breathing and how she shows pain
A list of the staff who have known her for the longest time
C.why: A documented baseline of her usual presentation and pain cues lets new staff recognise change, which is how illness shows in someone without speech.

whyNot.0: Activities matter for quality of life but do not help staff spot illness.
whyNot.1: Diagnostic codes say nothing about how Sian looks when well or unwell.
whyNot.3: Knowing who to ask helps, but the baseline itself must be written down for new staff.

reteach.title: The label is the start, not the plan
reteach.question: Two people both have a 'moderate learning disability'. Why might their support plans look completely different?

blocks.body: Severity is a broad band. One person with a moderate learning disability may travel alone on a known bus route but need help with money; another may manage money with an app but need support with personal care. The support plan comes from adaptive functioning: what this person can do, and where they need help.

blocks.text: Do not convert severity into a 'mental age' or into a capacity judgement. Both are assessed for the real person and the real decision.

explain.body: Mild, moderate, severe and profound. All are lifelong. Moving up the scale, people need more support with mobility, personal care and communication.

test.q: Which statement about the levels of learning disability is accurate?
options: Mild learning disability usually resolves in adult life
Each level is lifelong, with support needs rising by level
A person moves to a milder level after leaving school
The levels describe how intelligent a person will become
test.why: Mencap: learning disability can be mild, moderate, severe or profound, and in all cases it is lifelong; support needs generally increase with severity.

whyNot.0: No level resolves; a learning disability is lifelong.
whyNot.2: Leaving school does not change the level, though skills can grow.
whyNot.3: Levels describe current functioning and support, not a fixed prediction.

explain.body: Older IQ bands (for example about 50 to 69 for mild) are approximate. ICD-11 assesses intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour together. Support plans rest on adaptive skills: self-care, communication, money, travel and safety.

test.q: A community nurse is planning support for Joel, 33, who is moving into his first flat. Which assessment will be most useful?
options: A repeat IQ test to confirm his level
A review of his genetic test results
A record of his school exam results
An assessment of his everyday living skills
test.why: Adaptive (everyday) skills show exactly where Joel needs help in his new home.

whyNot.0: An IQ score does not show which daily tasks he needs help with.
whyNot.1: Genetic results may guide health checks but not daily support.
whyNot.2: Exam results do not describe independent living skills.

explain.body: A profound learning disability plus physical and/or sensory impairments and complex health needs, usually with very limited speech. Care depends on knowing the person's baseline and communication through behaviour, sounds and expression.

test.q: Which description best fits profound and multiple learning disabilities?
options: A profound learning disability with physical or sensory impairments and complex health needs
A moderate learning disability with autism and a co-occurring mental health condition
A profound learning disability that is caused by more than one identified genetic syndrome
Several specific learning difficulties, such as dyslexia and dyspraxia, in the same person
test.why: PMLD combines a profound learning disability with additional physical and/or sensory impairments and complex health needs.

whyNot.1: PMLD involves a profound, not moderate, learning disability with physical or sensory impairment.
whyNot.2: 'Multiple' refers to additional disabilities, not multiple genetic causes.
whyNot.3: Specific learning difficulties do not affect general intellect and are not PMLD.

explain.body: LeDeR 2023 (republished January 2026): average age at death 63 overall, 58 for people with severe or profound learning disability, who were more likely to die of something treatable. Missed symptoms and diagnostic overshadowing drive this gap.

test.q: What was the average age at death for people with a severe or profound learning disability in the republished LeDeR 2023 report?
options: 63 years
58 years
68 years
52 years
test.why: LeDeR 2023 (republished 27 January 2026): 58 for people with a severe or profound learning disability, against 63 overall.

whyNot.0: 63 is the average for all people with a learning disability in 2023.
whyNot.2: 68 is not a LeDeR 2023 figure for this group.
whyNot.3: 52 is lower than the reported figure of 58.
